There is genuine expert disagreement on whether pregnant women should follow a vegan diet. Belgium's Royal Academy of Medicine explicitly recommended that "children, teens, pregnant women and nursing mothers do not follow a vegan diet," citing "unavoidable" nutritional shortcomings and the risk of "irreversible" harms, including deficiencies in proteins, essential fatty acids, vitamins D and B12, and calcium [d1]. In contrast, a peer-reviewed study indexed on PubMed found that "pregnant and breastfeeding vegan women can meet all of their nutrient needs on a vegan diet that includes a variety of plant foods and reliable sources of vitamin B12 and vitamin D," with several scientific societies issuing favorable position statements on vegan diets during pregnancy [d2]. Similarly, WebMD states that "a well-planned vegan diet can provide everything you need during all stages of your life, including when you're pregnant or breastfeeding," and notes potential protective effects against preeclampsia and gestational diabetes [d7]. The U.S. Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics and other nutrition societies have also issued official statements backing the safety of vegan diets during pregnancy, provided they are carefully planned [d5]. A 2015 study cited by BabyDoppler concluded that "vegan-vegetarian diets may be considered safe during pregnancy if nutritional requirements are met," though it acknowledged a lack of research in this area [d4]. The consensus among those who support vegan pregnancy diets is that careful planning, supplementation (especially B12, D, iron, and calcium), and medical monitoring are essential [d2, d5, d6, d7].
